grammar.name: The Hebrew Alphabet (א–ס), Vowels (Nikud), and Prefix Letters
grammar.explanation: Hebrew is written right-to-left, exactly like Arabic. The alphabet has 22 consonant letters; vowel marks (nikud) act like Arabic ḥarakāt. Letters א, ה, ו, י can double as long vowels (ḥurūf al-'illa). Five letters change shape at the end of a word (sofit), such as kaf (כ/ך), mem (מ/ם), and nun (נ/ן). Just like Arabic attached particles (بـ, الـ, وـ, لـ, من), single-letter prepositions and conjunctions attach directly to the next word: בְּ־ (in/at = بـ), הַ־ (the = الـ), וְ־ (and = وـ), לְ־ (to/for = لـ), and מִ־ (from = من). Bet (ב) sounds like /b/ with a dot (dagesh) and /v/ without.
grammar.pattern:
Prefixes: בְּ־ (in) / הַ־ (the) / וְ־ (and) + מִלָּה (word)
Sofit (endings): כ → ך | מ → ם | נ → ן
Nikud: ַ / ָ = /a/ | ֶ / ֵ = /e/ | ִ = /i/ | ֹ / וֹ = /o/ | ֻ / וּ = /u/

grammar.name: German Core Patterns: Capitalization, Genders & Verb Position
grammar.explanation: German differs from English in key ways: 1. All nouns are capitalized, whether at the start or in the middle of a sentence. 2. Every noun has a grammatical gender: masculine (der), feminine (die), or neuter (das). 3. Special characters exist: the umlauts (ä, ö, ü) and the sharp 's' (ß). 4. German has no continuous tense (ich arbeite means both 'I work' and 'I am working'). 5. In main declarative clauses, the conjugated verb is always the second element.
grammar.pattern:
Nouns: CAPITALIZED (der Mann, die Frau, das Haus)
Genders: der (masc.) | die (fem.) | das (neut.)
Verb position 2: [Position 1] + [Verb] + [Subject/Rest...]
No continuous aspect: 'Ich lerne' = I learn / I am learning

grammar.name: Regular verbs in the present tense
grammar.explanation: To form the present tense of regular verbs in German, you take the infinitive (e.g., wohnen), remove the ending '-en' to find the stem ('wohn-'), and add the personal ending according to the subject. grammar.name: Final Letters (Otiyot Sofiyot) and Hard/Soft Pronunciation
grammar.explanation: Hebrew has five letters that change their shape when they appear at the very end of a word: ך (kaf), ם (mem), ן (nun), ף (pei), ץ (tzadi). Notice how ף (pei sofit) and ך (kaf sofit) at the end of words sound like /f/ and /ch/, similar to Arabic sound positions (ف and خ). Furthermore, letters like ב, כ, פ change pronunciation depending on a dot (dagesh): with a dot they are stop sounds (/b/, /k/, /p/), and without a dot they become fricatives (/v/, /ch/, /f/), perfectly mirroring Arabic letter developments.

פּ (/p/) -> פֹּה | פ (/f/) -> דַּף

grammar.name: Verb variations and irregular verbs (Präsens)
grammar.explanation: Most German verbs add standard endings to the stem, but some have spelling variations in the present tense, affecting du and er/sie/es. Stems ending in -d or -t (arbeiten) add an extra -e- before endings (du arbeitest, er arbeitet). Stems ending in -s, -ss, -ß, or -z (reisen, heißen) add only -t for du (du reist, du heißt). Irregular verbs change their stem vowel only for du and er/sie/es: a becomes ä (fahren → du fährst), e becomes i (treffen → du triffst; essen → du isst; nehmen → du nimmst), or e becomes ie (sehen → er sieht; lesen → er liest).
grammar.pattern:
arbeiten: du arbeitest, er arbeitet (-d/-t stem: +e-)
reisen: du reist, er reist (-s/-ß/-z stem: +t only)
a → ä: du fährst, er fährt (fahren, schlafen)
e → i/ie: du triffst, er liest (treffen, lesen)

grammar.name: Irregular verbs: haben and sein
grammar.explanation: In German, irregular verbs often change their stem vowel in the present tense for du and er/sie/es, such as in 'Der Freund isst einen Apfel' (essen -> isst). The verb haben drops the stem 'b' for du hast and er/sie/es hat, but stays regular for all other forms. The verb sein is completely irregular (ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist, etc.) and must be learned by heart. Note that German has only one present tense: there is no continuous form like 'I am going'.

haben: ich habe | du hast | er/sie/es hat | wir haben | ihr habt | sie/Sie haben
sein:  ich bin  | du bist | er/sie/es ist | wir sind  | ihr seid | sie/Sie sind

grammar.name: Separable Verbs in the Present Tense
grammar.explanation: Separable verbs consist of a prefix and a main verb (e.g., auf + stehen). In present tense main clauses, the main verb stays in second position and conjugates normally, while the split-off prefix moves to the very end of the clause. In sentences with two main clauses, each prefix goes to the end of its respective clause. Common separable prefixes include ab-, an-, auf-, aus-, ein-, mit-, vor-, and zu-. Note that prefixes like be-, er-, ge-, and ver- are inseparable and remain attached to the verb.
grammar.pattern:
Position 2: Main verb  |  End of clause: Prefix
Subject + [Conjugated Verb] + ... + [Prefix].
Jens + steht + um halb acht Uhr + auf.
Clause 1 [Verb ... Prefix 1], und / aber Clause 2 [Verb ... Prefix 2].

unit.title: The imperative
unit.objective: give instructions and make requests with du, ihr and Sie

lesson.title: Der Imperativ
lesson.goal: Give instructions and make requests using du, ihr, and Sie.

grammar.name: The Imperative (du, ihr, Sie)
grammar.explanation: Separable verbs split off their prefix and place it at the end of the sentence. For example, Nico steht um fünf Uhr morgens auf. The imperative gives commands with the verb in first position. For 'du', drop the ending -en and pronoun (Komm!); add -e for stems ending in -d/-t (Warte!), keep e->i stem changes (Sprich!), but drop a->ä umlauts (Fahr!). For 'ihr', add -t to the stem without pronoun (Kommt!). For formal 'Sie', use the infinitive followed by Sie (Kommen Sie!). Separable prefixes go to the end (Fang an!). Irregular 'sein' uses Sei!, Seid!, and Seien Sie!.
grammar.pattern:
du: Stem (+ -e) | Lies! / Warte! / Fang ... an!
ihr: Stem + -t | Lest! / Wartet! / Fangt ... an!
Sie: Infinitive + Sie | Lesen Sie! / Warten Sie! / Fangen Sie an!
sein: Sei! (du) | Seid! (ihr) | Seien Sie! (Sie)

unit.title: Asking questions
unit.objective: ask yes/no and W-questions with correct word order

lesson.title: Fragen stellen: W-Fragen und Ja/Nein-Fragen
lesson.goal: Ask yes/no and W-questions using correct German word order in both formal and informal contexts.

grammar.name: W-Questions and Yes/No Questions
grammar.explanation: In the last unit, we learned that imperatives give direct commands, like 'Fahr mehr mit dem Fahrrad!' for du or 'Warten Sie bitte!' for Sie. Remember to drop verb endings for informal commands and place the verb first for formal commands. In this unit, we form questions. W-questions start with a question word (wer, was, wo, woher, wohin, wie, wann) in position 1, followed by the verb in position 2, then the subject. Yes/no questions move the finite verb directly to position 1, with the subject right after. Use 'wie' for names, addresses, and time. German does not use the auxiliary 'do'.
grammar.pattern:
W-Question: Question Word + Verb + Subject + ...?
(z.B. Wo wohnt er? / Wie ist Ihre E-Mail-Adresse?)
Yes/No Question: Verb + Subject + ...?
(z.B. Sprechen Sie Deutsch? / Kommt Timo wirklich aus Bremen?)

unit.title: Articles
unit.objective: use definite, indefinite and negative articles (der, ein, kein)

lesson.title: Nomen und Artikel
lesson.goal: The learner can correctly use definite and indefinite articles (der, die, das, ein, eine) to refer to specific and unspecific nouns in German.

grammar.name: Definite and Indefinite Articles
grammar.explanation: To ask questions in German, place the verb first for yes/no questions or after the question word. Ensure correct subject-verb agreement, for example: Der Mann und die Frau haben Zeit. Definite articles (der, die, das, plural die) refer to specific nouns. Indefinite articles (ein, eine, ein) refer to unspecific nouns and have no plural form. Definite articles are required with seasons (der Sommer), certain countries (die Schweiz), street names, and abstract nouns (das Leben), but omitted for playing instruments. Indefinite articles are omitted for occupations and nationalities unless an adjective is present (ein guter Rechtsanwalt). Das or dies functions as 'this/that is' or 'these/those are'.
grammar.pattern:
Masc: der / ein Mann
Fem:  die / eine Frau
Neut: das / ein Kind
Plur: die / --- Kinder

unit.title: Nouns and gender
unit.objective: predict a noun's gender from its ending and learn nouns with their article
unit.book: Basic German, unit 9: Nouns and gender (pp. 57–63)

lesson.title: Nomen und Genus
lesson.goal: Predict a noun's gender from its ending or category and learn nouns with their articles.

grammar.name: Nouns and Gender (Nomen und Genus)
grammar.explanation: German uses three definite articles for singular nouns: der (masculine), die (feminine), and das (neuter), which all become die in the plural. Correctly identifying these articles is essential because they show grammatical gender. In German, gender can often be predicted by word endings or semantic categories. Nouns ending in -ig, -ismus, -ling, -or (and days, seasons, car makes) are masculine (der). Nouns ending in -ei, -heit, -keit, -ung, -schaft, -tät, -ie, -ik, -ion (and female persons, trees, flowers) are feminine (die). Nouns ending in -chen, -lein, -ma, -ment, -o, -um (and young persons, metals, hotels) are neuter (das). In compound nouns, the final noun always determines the gender of the entire word. Remember: all German nouns are capitalized!
grammar.pattern:
der (masculine): -ig, -ismus, -ling, -or | days, seasons, cars
die (feminine): -ei, -heit, -keit, -ung, -schaft, -tät | female persons
das (neuter): -chen, -lein, -ma, -ment, -o, -um | young persons
Compound: die Reise + der Pass -> der Reisepass

lesson.title: Plural der Nomen
lesson.goal: Form the plural of the main German noun groups accurately across masculine, feminine, neuter, and foreign nouns.

grammar.name: Plural of Nouns (Plural der Nomen)
grammar.explanation: In German, every noun has a specific gender: masculine (der), feminine (die), or neuter (das). Learning a noun with its gender is essential because gender indicates how its plural is formed. German uses several plural patterns: most masculine nouns add -e or -¨e; about 90% of feminine nouns add -n or -en; neuter nouns commonly add -e or -¨er. Nouns ending in -er, -el, -en, -chen, or -lein take no ending (sometimes adding an umlaut). Imported foreign words from English or French usually take -s.
grammar.pattern:
m: +e / +¨e (der Tag -> die Tage, der Zug -> die Züge)
f: +n / +en / +¨e (die Tasse -> die Tassen, die Stadt -> die Städte)
n: +e / +¨er (das Jahr -> die Jahre, das Buch -> die Bücher)
Foreign: +s (das Handy -> die Handys)
-er/-el/-en/-chen/-lein: no ending / +¨ (das Zimmer -> die Zimmer, der Apfel -> die Äpfel)

unit.title: The four cases
unit.objective: explain what the four cases do in a sentence
unit.book: Basic German, unit 11: The four cases (pp. 71–76)

lesson.title: Die vier Fälle
lesson.goal: The learner can explain what the four cases do in a sentence and name the three determining factors.

grammar.name: The four cases
grammar.explanation: Remember from our last unit that nouns change their plural forms to show more than one. In German, nouns also play different roles in a sentence, which are signalled by cases that change the endings of accompanying words like articles. There are four cases. The nominative is used for the subject (the agent doing the action). The accusative is for the direct object (the receiver of the action). The dative is for the indirect object (to or for whom the action is done). The genitive shows possession or a relationship between two nouns. Case is determined by three factors: the role of the noun in the sentence, the verb, and prepositions.
grammar.pattern:
Nominative: Subject (Der Mann liest.)
Accusative: Direct Object (den Roman)
Dative: Indirect Object (dem Freund)
Genitive: Possession (des Mannes)

unit.objective: identify the subject and use the nominative correctly

lesson.title: Der Nominativ: Das Subjekt im Satz
lesson.goal: Identify the subject of a sentence and use nominative determiners correctly.

grammar.name: The Nominative Case (Der Nominativ)
grammar.explanation: German nouns change according to their case, which depends on the role of the noun in the sentence, the verb, and prepositions. These four cases alter articles and endings to show who or what performs or receives an action. German uses the nominative case when the noun is the subject—the person or thing doing the action. You also use the nominative after the verbs sein ('to be') and werden ('to become'). Determiners, such as der Artikel (definite articles), indefinite articles, possessives, and negative kein, take specific nominative forms. To spot the subject, ask 'who or what is doing the action?'; remember that the subject does not have to be at the beginning of the sentence.
grammar.pattern:
masculine: der / ein / mein / kein Mann
feminine: die / eine / meine / keine Frau
neuter: das / ein / mein / kein Kind
plural: die / — / meine / keine Gäste
Special verbs: [Subject] + sein / werden + [Nominative]

lesson.title: Der Akkusativ
lesson.goal: The learner will be able to use the accusative case for direct objects and after accusative prepositions.

grammar.name: The accusative case (Der Akkusativ)
grammar.explanation: The nominative case marks the subject performing the action (der, die, das; ein, eine, ein). It shows who or what is doing something in the sentence. In contrast, the accusative case marks the direct object (the receiver of the action) and follows specific prepositions: bis, durch, für, gegen, ohne, um. Only masculine determiners change ending in the accusative: der becomes den, and ein becomes einen (e.g., einen Regenschirm, not ein). Neuter (das/ein), feminine (die/eine), and plural forms remain identical to the nominative.
grammar.pattern:
masculine: der -> den | ein -> einen | mein -> meinen
feminine:  die -> die | eine -> eine  | meine -> meine
neuter:    das -> das | ein -> ein    | mein -> mein
plural:    die -> die | —             | meine -> meine
prepositions + Akk: bis, durch, für, gegen, ohne, um
